Stage 3 · Reading

The week I stopped being sensible

A first-person account of fourteen days that did not go to plan.

🏔🌿
1 · Before you read. The writer calls herself “sensible”, not “boring”. What does that choice of word suggest?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The week I stopped being sensible

Written for this course.

1Until two years ago I had never slept anywhere without a lock on the door. I was not an adventurous person and I had never pretended to be one. My holidays were cities, museums and a return flight booked before I left. Then my sister paid for a fourteen-day trek through a remote valley in the north, told me afterwards, and refused to discuss it. Her argument was that I needed to step out of my comfort zone. Mine was that I had a job, a cat and no boots.

2By the end of the first afternoon I had already stopped speaking. We had been walking for six hours, my bag weighed more than I had estimated, and the physical side of it was worse than anything I had prepared for. Nobody had warned me that the difficulty of a trek is not the distance but the small decisions: whether to stop now or in twenty minutes, whether the pain in your heel is a blister or the boot. My sister, who had done this sort of thing before, made a poor companion that first day. She kept pointing out that the views were stunning, which they were, and which did not help.

3The trip turned on day four. We had lost the path an hour earlier and had been arguing about the map when an old man appeared from nowhere with two dogs. Neither of us spoke his language and he had no interest in ours. He looked at the map, laughed at it, and walked us to the col. There he pointed at our destination, a white village on the far side of the valley, and went home. The whole encounter lasted less than an hour and it is the only part of the fortnight I would call remarkable. Neither of us had done anything to deserve it. That is what I have thought about most since.

4What surprised me afterwards was how little of it was about courage. I finished the walk because turning back had become more trouble than going on, and that is not the same thing. There was no moment on any of the fourteen days when I chose the difficult option over the easy one; there was simply never an easy one available. People who describe a trek as a feat, or who come home calling themselves explorers, have usually skipped that part of the story. Nobody sent us on a mission. We were two women with a map neither of us could read.

5Something did change, though, and it changed later than I expected. By the second week I had taken over the route, the food and the timing, not out of determination but because my sister had stopped doing it and somebody had to. I was carrying a responsibility I had spent forty years arranging my life to avoid, and it turned out to weigh about as much as the bag. On the last evening I wandered round a town I had never heard of, alone, in the dark, for two hours, and enjoyed every minute of it.

6I am not a different person. I still book the return flight first. But I am determined to go back, and this time I have booked it myself, which my sister says proves her point and which I am not going to admit.

Text A · Fourteen days I had not agreed to

Written for this course.

My holidays were cities, museums and a return flight booked before I left. Then my sister paid for a fourteen-day trek through a remote valley in the north, told me afterwards, and refused to discuss it. Her argument was that I needed to step out of my comfort zone. Mine was that I had a job, a cat and no boots.

By the end of the first afternoon I had already stopped speaking. We had been walking for six hours, my bag weighed more than I had estimated, and the physical side of it was worse than anything I had prepared for. Nobody had warned me that the difficulty of a trek is not the distance but the small decisions: whether to stop now or in twenty minutes, whether the pain in your heel is a blister or the boot. Text B · What it was not

Written for this course.

What surprised me afterwards was how little of it was about courage. I finished the walk because turning back had become more trouble than going on, and that is not the same thing. There was no moment on any of the fourteen days when I chose the difficult option over the easy one; there was simply never an easy one available. People who describe a trek as a feat, or who come home calling themselves explorers, have usually skipped that part of the story. Nobody had sent us on a mission. We were two women with a map neither of us could read.

Something did change, though, and it changed later than I expected. By the second week I had taken over the route, the food and the timing, not out of determination but because my sister had stopped doing it and somebody had to. I was carrying a responsibility I had spent forty years arranging my life to avoid, and it turned out to weigh about as much as the bag. On the last evening I wandered round a town I had never heard of, alone, in the dark, for two hours, and enjoyed every minute of it.

I am not a different person. I still book the return flight first, and I have not thrown away the lock on the door. But I am determined to go back, and this time I have booked it myself, which my sister says proves her point and which I am not going to admit. If she had asked me first, I would have said no, and I would have been wrong; I am prepared to accept that much and no more.

Three forms, three jobs: the events, the background, and everything that happened before the story started.

4 · One moment, four ways of telling it.
The path disappeared.  →  the event itself.
We were walking when the path disappeared.  →  what was going on around it.
We had been walking for six hours when it disappeared.  →  how long it had been going on.

1 · Read the explanation.
Three layers in one story

English tells past stories in layers. The past simple carries the events themselves, one after another, in the order they happened. The past continuous supplies whatever was already going on around them: the weather, the noise, the activity that got interrupted. The past perfect steps back behind the story and reports something that had happened before it began.

The past perfect is not a politer or more advanced past simple. It is a marker of order, and you use it when the order matters and nothing else in the sentence makes it clear. In She booked it and told me afterwards, the word afterwards does the work, so no past perfect appears.

Three questions to ask before you choose
  • Is this an event in the story, or before it? In the story → past simple. Before it → past perfect.
  • Was it finished, or still running? Finished → simple. Still running at that moment → continuous: we had been walking for six hours.
  • Does anything else already show the order? Then, afterwards, before, and — if one of these is present, the past simple is usually enough.
2 · Study the examples.
JobExample

Two things to watch

1 — The past perfect is relative, not distant. It does not mean a very long time ago. It means before the other past thing I am talking about. Something five minutes earlier still takes it.

2 — Do not use it for every earlier event. Once the order is established, English drops back into the past simple: We had lost the path. An old man appeared, walked us to the col and went home.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Three forms, three jobs

A story in English is built out of three layers. The past simple carries the events in the order they happened: She booked it and told me afterwards. Each new past simple verb moves the clock forward, which is why a run of them reads as a sequence even without then.

The past continuous does not move the clock. It paints what was already going on when an event arrived: It was raining when we set off. With when and while the pattern is nearly fixed — the longer action takes the continuous, the interrupting one takes the simple: We were walking along the ridge when the path disappeared. Two continuous verbs joined by while mean the two things ran side by side: While I was packing, she was checking the forecast.

The past perfect reaches back to something that was already true before the story reached that point: My bag weighed more than I had estimated. It is the only one of the three that changes the order of telling without changing the order of events.

Where each one stops working

State verbs resist the continuous in the past exactly as they do in the present: I knew the way, not I was knowing. And the past continuous never carries the plot — a story told entirely in it never gets anywhere.

The past perfect is needed only when the order would otherwise be misread. After before and after the sequence is already clear from the conjunction, so the past simple is usually enough: After we set off, the weather closed in. Overusing the past perfect is the commonest B2 fault in narrative writing: use it for the step back, then return to the past simple for the story itself.

Had never plus a past participle is the standard way of giving a first time: I had never slept outdoors before that night. Note the before — it is doing real work, and the sentence is about the moment in the story, not about now.

Errors to watch: While I walked, the rain was starting → While I was walking, the rain started · I was knowing the path → I knew · After I had arrived, I had unpacked and I had eaten → the story itself takes the past simple.

1 · Read the model.
Model · an account of one difficult day

Before last September I had never spent a night in a place I could not leave on my own. I am not an adventurous person; I had simply agreed to something in March that I had not thought about since.

The fourth day was the one that mattered. We had been climbing since five and the cloud had come down, so we were walking through white air with nothing on either side. At about eleven I realised I had left the map in the hut. My companion said nothing, which was worse than anything she could have said.

We sat on a rock for two hours. By the time the cloud lifted we had eaten everything we were carrying, and the valley below us turned out to be the wrong one.

I would like to write that I discovered some determination in myself that afternoon. What I actually discovered was that I had been treating the whole trip as something happening to me. From the fifth day I carried the map.
